metadata.note: The Missisquoi Railroad, St. Albans - Richford, Vermont (27.5 mi), opened 1871 and run for most of its passenger life by the Central Vermont. One line, four features with identical geometry, split by who ran the trains: Vermont Central 1871-1872, Central Vermont 1873-1877, Missisquoi Railroad (probable own-name operation) 1878-1888, Central Vermont 1888-1938. Sheldon Junction was a crossing with the St. Johnsbury & Lake Champlain (Lamoille Valley), and Richford the junction with the separate Missisquoi & Clyde Rivers / Canadian Pacific line to Newport; neither is part of this layer. The CV main line north of Essex Junction through St. Albans is not drawn under the CV name elsewhere in data/, so this branch currently hangs off a St. Albans the CV layer does not reach.

geometry_quality.missisquoi-vc-st-albans-richford: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap, no straight-line legs. Traced 27.3 mi St. Albans station - Richford against a documented 27.5 mi (branchline.uk SL196 chainage; the Feb 1952 Official Guide gives 27.3, en.wikipedia 27.48), i.e. within 1%. opstrace mileage by operator: 27.3 mi on ways tagged old_railway_operator=CN (the CV's last owner), 0 mi on any other operator's rails -- in particular 0 mi on the B&M-tagged Lamoille Valley Rail Trail crossed at Sheldon Junction, and nothing beyond Richford onto the CP/Missisquoi & Clyde Rivers line. Of that, ~26.3 mi is the Missisquoi Valley Rail Trail itself (the state plan's 26.3-mi trail length), ~0.7 mi abandoned CN-tagged track on the St. Albans approach, and ~0.3 mi active CN/NECR track at St. Albans station, where the branch left the main line just north of the depot. Every waypoint lies within 0.2 km of the line (St. Albans station 0.0, Sheldon Springs 0.1, Sheldon Junction 0.2, North Sheldon 0.1, Enosburg Falls 0.2, East Berkshire 0.1) except Richford, 0.8 km from Nominatim's village-centre point: the trace ends where the rail trail ends at the south edge of the village, so the last few hundred metres into the Richford depot are not drawn. 127 points after Douglas-Peucker (8 m) and reversal trimming. LATER-ALIGNMENT CAVEAT (Rule 2): this is the grade as abandoned in 1990-92, drawn back to 1871. No period valuation or survey map was consulted; the rural alignment is assumed unchanged since construction, and the St. Albans yard approach in particular may have been rearranged after 1871. Vermont Central era 1871-1872.

not_yet_sourced: OPERATOR 1878-1888 IS PROBABLE, NOT PROVEN. The Missisquoi Railroad / Missisquoi Valley Railroad is drawn as its own operator on the strength of 1880, 1885 and 1887 newspaper items (own ticket checks, own depot, timetables listed apart from the CV's divisions). Against: Green-Mountain Freeman 22 Dec 1880 lists the 'Missisquoi road, 28 miles' among roads the Central Vermont 'now controls'; and en.wikipedia says the Connecticut & Passumpsic Rivers took it over 15 Nov 1877, judged a conflation with the separate Missisquoi & Clyde Rivers (no newspaper support found). Passenger SERVICE in 1878-1888 is confirmed. Next sources: Poor's Manual 1878-1887 'Missisquoi' entries; Vermont Railroad Commissioner annual reports 1878-1886.

Last passenger year 1938 (11 Nov 1938) rests on a single secondary source, the VTrans MVRT Management Plan draft (June 2026, p. 9, unfootnoted). Consistent with the 1924 timetable, the 1939 Official Guide absence and the Feb 1952 Guide freight-only notice, but not itself primary. Fallback if rejected: 1924 as last confirmed year. Confirm via Lindsell, Rail Lines of Northern New England p. 327, or a St. Albans Messenger 'last train' story (Nov 1938).
End of the first CV lease, 15 Nov 1877, rests on en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia only.
Re-lease date to the CV: de.wikipedia 30 June 1888 vs en.wikipedia's implied Dec 1886 (that is the Missisquoi Valley reorganization); the Middlebury Register 21 Sept 1888 report supports 1888.
Opening-date conflict: 1871 (three contemporary newspapers, adopted) vs Dec 1872 (UVM) vs 1 July 1873 (de.wikipedia; 2026 state plan 'completed in 1873').
All headway_min and avg_speed_kmh values are estimates; the only frequency found is the secondary 1916-1924 peak of six weekday passenger trains.
Geometry: last ~0.8 km into the Richford depot not drawn (the rail trail stops short); the 1871 alignment, especially the St. Albans yard approach, is assumed equal to the 1990s abandoned grade.
metadata.freight_only_audit: Nothing drawn after 1938: freight-only operation 1938-1984 (then locally to 1990/1992) is mentioned in notes as context only. Industrial spurs (Sheldon Springs paper mill, Richford feed mill) not drawn.
metadata.horsecar_audit: Not applicable: steam railroad from its 1871 opening.

segments.note: The Missisquoi Railroad, St. Albans to Richford via Sheldon Springs, Sheldon Junction, North Sheldon, Enosburgh Falls and East Berkshire, was run from the start by the Vermont Central and Vermont & Canada trustees and managers as their 'Eastern Division' (Feb 1871 operating order); the Missisquoi company did not run its own trains at opening. First regular passenger trip St. Albans - Sheldon on a Monday in late June 1871; track to Richford by mid-September; formal opening of the whole road c. 30 Sept 1871, 'Trains will hereafter run regularly over the entire road'. In 1871 only St. Albans - Sheldon was open until the autumn, but the whole line is drawn for the year. Oct 1872: the trustees took a durable lease at forty per cent of gross receipts. The segment ends 1872 because the Vermont Central was renamed Central Vermont on 2 Nov 1872 -- the same trains continued; this file follows vermont_central_railroad.geojson in splitting at the rename (VC to 1872, CV from 1873). OPENING-DATE CONFLICT recorded, not silently resolved: UVM says completed Dec 1872, de.wikipedia 1 July 1873, the 2026 state trail plan 'completed in 1873'; three contemporary 1871 newspapers outrank them, and the later dates look like the lease/completion. Headway (about two trains each way a day) and speed are estimates, not sourced. All four features in this file share identical geometry, split by operator era (CLAUDE.md Rule 4).
sources: Segment-level: start year, the Vermont Central operation and the 1872 lease from contemporary newspapers -- Rutland Weekly Herald 23 Feb 1871 p.3 (operating order), 29 Jun 1871 p.1 (first regular passenger trip), 21 Sep 1871 p.5, 14 Dec 1871, 18 Oct 1872 p.1 (lease); Green-Mountain Freeman 19 Jul 1871 p.3 and 4 Oct 1871 p.3 (formal opening). End year is the 2 Nov 1872 rename, per repo convention. Headway NOT sourced.

segments.note: Central Vermont Railroad (the renamed Vermont Central; company string 'Central Vermont Railway' so the whole CV succession shares one colour, as in vermont_central_railroad.geojson) as lessee -- formal lease July 1873. Passenger service confirmed in 1873 (an 'up train' killed a man near Gordon's Corner, Orleans County Monitor 27 Oct 1873) and 1876 (four stations in the 1876 Pathfinder per branchline.uk). From 1874 through New York - Newport trains ran 'over the Missisquoi railroad' to Richford and on over the Missisquoi & Clyde Rivers (Rutland Daily Globe 27 Jul 1874) -- context; the Richford - Newport road is a different railroad and not drawn here. Ends 1877: the CV lease was dissolved / CV operation ended 15 Nov 1877 (en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia agree on the day; both secondary, no primary found for the date). The next feature starts 1878, the first full year of the following operator. Headway and speed are estimates, not sourced. All four features in this file share identical geometry, split by operator era (CLAUDE.md Rule 4).

Headway NOT sourced.

segments.note: PASSENGER SERVICE in these years is CONFIRMED: no trains 'from the Missisquoi road' reached the St. Albans butter market on a snow day (Orleans County Monitor 3 Feb 1879); camp-meeting fares 1880; an excursion 'from the Missisquoi road' to the Morrisville camp meeting (Burlington Weekly Free Press 22 Aug 1884); Missisquoi timetables in the 1885 CV folder. THE OPERATOR IS PROBABLE, NOT PROVEN. This feature reads 1878-1888 as own-name operation by the Missisquoi Railroad (reorganized as the Missisquoi Valley Railroad 24 Dec 1886 -- a corporate change only, not a split), owned c. 1880-1884 by Bradley Barlow of St. Albans. Evidence FOR: Aug 1880 the Missisquoi carried camp-meeting passengers and 'the Central Vermont will honor the checks of the Missisquoi road' -- two roads, two sets of tickets (Green-Mountain Freeman 18 Aug 1880); Feb 1880 Barlow bought the bonds and 'thus become its owner' (Burlington Weekly Free Press 27 Feb 1880); Oct 1885 the CV folder printed timetables for its own divisions 'as well as on the Missisquoi road' (BWFP 9 Oct 1885); Aug 1887 'the Missisquoi Valley Rail road depot at Enosburg Falls' (Orleans County Monitor 1 Aug 1887); Dec 1887 'the Missisquoi Valley road will furnish free return passage over its line', named apart from the CV (St. Johnsbury Caledonian 29 Dec 1887). Evidence AGAINST: a Dec 1880 list of roads the 'Central Vermont Company now controls' includes 'Missisquoi road, 28 miles' (Green-Mountain Freeman 22 Dec 1880) -- possibly financial or traffic control rather than operation, but a conflict. en.wikipedia says the Connecticut & Passumpsic Rivers RR 'took it over' 15 Nov 1877; no newspaper support was found, and the C&PR's 1877-78 seizure/receivership was of the separate Missisquoi & CLYDE RIVERS road (Richford - Newport), so that sentence is judged a conflation of the two Missisquoi roads. Ends 1888: the CV re-leased the Missisquoi Valley (de.wikipedia: 30 June 1888; reported in the Middlebury Register 21 Sept 1888). Both this feature and the following Central Vermont feature include 1888, following the repo norm for a mid-year lease (e.g. watertown_rome_railroad.geojson's RW&O 1861-1891 / NYC 1891-). Colour #2FBF56 is new to this file; no other company in data/ uses it. Headway and speed are estimates, not sourced. All four features in this file share identical geometry, split by operator era (CLAUDE.md Rule 4).
sources: Segment-level: service and the probable operator from Chronicling America items -- Orleans County Monitor 3 Feb 1879 p.3, 1 Aug 1887 p.3; Green-Mountain Freeman 18 Aug 1880 p.3, 22 Dec 1880 p.2 (the conflicting 'controls' item); Burlington Weekly Free Press 27 Feb 1880 p.4, 22 Aug 1884 p.1, 9 Oct 1885 p.5; St. Johnsbury Caledonian 29 Dec 1887 p.4; Middlebury Register 21 Sept 1888 p.4 (end: CV re-lease). Start year 1878 is the first full year after the 15 Nov 1877 end of the CV lease (en/de wikipedia). Operator PROBABLE, not proven. Headway NOT sourced.

segments.note: Central Vermont as lessee from the 1888 re-lease (de.wikipedia 30 June 1888; Middlebury Register 21 Sept 1888), owner from 15 April 1899 after the 29 Sept 1898 merger -- the CV was already running the trains, so the purchase is not a split; nor is the 1923 Grand Trunk -> Canadian National change. Both this feature and the preceding Missisquoi feature include 1888 (repo norm for a mid-year lease). Known as the CV's Missisquoi Valley Division, later the Richford Branch / Richford Subdivision. Every station appears in the CV public timetables of 1893, 1916 and 1924 (branchline.uk), the 1924 local also stopping at 16 highway-crossing flag stops. Peak 1916-1924 of six weekday passenger trains including a daily milk train (state plan citing Lindsell p. 327); a combined mixed train from the early 1930s. END: passenger service ended 11 Nov 1938 per a SINGLE SECONDARY SOURCE, the Vermont Agency of Transportation's Missisquoi Valley Rail Trail Management Plan (DRAFT, June 2026, p. 9; the sentence carries no footnote of its own). It is consistent with every primary source read: present in the 1924 public timetable; absent from the 1939 Official Guide (absence alone proves nothing); 'Freight Service ... by rail' across CV Table 3 and a dagger (freight-only) on Enosburgh Falls in the Feb 1952 Official Guide. If the 1938 date is rejected, the conservative fallback is 1924 as the last primary-confirmed year. Context only, not drawn: freight continued after 1938 (Blue Seal Feeds at Richford, the Sheldon Springs paper mill) until the June 1984 Sheldon Junction bridge derailment, then locally each side until abandonment in 1990 (west) and 1992 (east); the grade is now the Missisquoi Valley Rail Trail. The 1952 Northern Bus Lines St. Albans - Richford coach is a bus. Headway (about three trains each way at the 1916-24 peak, fewer either side) and speed are estimates. All four features in this file share identical geometry, split by operator era (CLAUDE.md Rule 4).
sources: Segment-level: start from Middlebury Register 21 Sept 1888 p.4 and de.wikipedia (30 June 1888); service 1893/1916/1924 from the branchline.uk timetable letters; 1916-24 train count and early-1930s mixed train from the VTrans MVRT draft plan (citing Lindsell); end 11 Nov 1938 from the VTrans MVRT draft plan ONLY (single secondary source), consistent with the 1939 Guide absence and the Feb 1952 Official Guide CV Table 3 freight-only notice. Headway is an estimate.
Official Guide of the Railways, Feb 1952, CV Table 3 and index of stations (research/sources/official_guide_1952.txt in the historical-trains repo)
